unit.name: Catholic Christianity: Beliefs and Teachings
unit.subtitle: The Trinity, creation, incarnation, redemption and life after death

lessons.title: The Trinity and the Nicene Creed
lessons.description: One God as a Trinity of persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — expressed in the Nicene Creed (325 CE).
lessons.content_html:
One God, Three Persons

At the heart of Catholic Christianity is the belief that God is the Trinity — one God who exists as three co-equal and co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is not a belief in three separate gods. Catholic teaching insists firmly on the oneness of God alongside the three-ness of persons. The Nicene Creed opens with the declaration “We believe in one God” before naming the three persons in turn.

A common misconception is that Christians — and Catholics in particular — believe in three gods. The technical phrase that earns marks in an exam is “one God, three persons” or, in the language of the early Church, “one substance, three persons” (from the Latin una substantia, tres personae). Each person is distinct but not separate: the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, yet all three are fully God.

Key Fact

The Trinity: God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all things; God the Son (Jesus Christ) is the incarnate Word who redeems humanity; God the Holy Spirit is the presence of God active in the world and in believers today. One God, three persons — this is the foundational Catholic belief.

Scriptural Origins of the Trinity

The doctrine of the Trinity is rooted in scripture. At the baptism of Jesus, all three persons are present simultaneously: Jesus is baptised in the River Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends on him “like a dove”, and the voice of the Father speaks from heaven: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16–17). The Great Commission in Matthew 28:19 instructs the disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” — a single name held by three persons.

The Gospel of John deepens the Trinitarian picture. John 1:1 declares: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” This Logos (Word) was present at creation and became flesh in Jesus (John 1:14). Paul’s letters develop the idea of the Spirit dwelling in believers (Romans 8:9–11), completing the Trinitarian picture that the Church would later formalise.

By the early fourth century, debate had erupted within the Church about the exact relationship between the Father and the Son. A theologian called Arius argued that the Son was a created being — subordinate to the Father and not fully divine. This was widely held to be a serious error by the majority of bishops. Emperor Constantine convened the first ecumenical council at Nicaea in modern-day Turkey in 325 CE to settle the dispute.

The council condemned Arianism and produced the Nicene Creed — a formal statement of orthodox belief. The creed declares that the Son is “of one substance with the Father” (the Greek word homoousios), directly contradicting Arius. The creed was later refined at the Council of Constantinople (381 CE) to include a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit, reaching the form Catholics recite at Mass today.

The Three Persons and Their Roles

Catholic theology distinguishes the persons of the Trinity by their roles in relation to humanity. God the Father is the creator of heaven and earth. The Nicene Creed begins: “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.” The Father is the source and origin of all being, though always in relation to the Son and the Spirit.

God the Son is the eternal Word who took on human flesh — the incarnation. The creed describes him as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father.” The Son’s role is the redemption of humanity through his life, death and resurrection. The Holy Spirit is the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and (in Western Catholic teaching) from the Son also — the filioque clause that distinguishes Catholic from Eastern Orthodox theology.

All three major Christian traditions — Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant — affirm the Trinity as expressed in the Nicene Creed, so there is broad agreement on the core doctrine. The differences lie in emphasis and specific theological formulations.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity rejects the filioque addition (the teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son), which was inserted by the Western Church in the early medieval period. Orthodox theologians argue this addition distorts the balance between the three persons. Protestant Christianity shares the Nicene definition of the Trinity but may place greater emphasis on scripture as the primary source of Trinitarian knowledge, whereas Catholic theology gives significant weight to Church tradition and the Magisterium (the Church’s teaching authority) in interpreting the doctrine.

The Trinity in Catholic Life Today

The Trinity is not merely an abstract theological formula in Catholic life — it shapes daily practice. Catholics begin and end prayer with the Sign of the Cross: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The Mass opens and closes with Trinitarian language. Baptism is performed “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), bringing the new Christian into relationship with all three persons. The Magisterium — the Church’s official teaching body — holds that the Trinitarian faith cannot be separated from Christian life: to know God is to know him as Father, Son and Spirit.

In parishes across Britain today, the Nicene Creed is recited aloud by the whole congregation at Mass every Sunday. For many Catholics at Westminster Cathedral in London or at their local parish church, the creed is not experienced as doctrine alone but as a communal act of worship — a shared declaration of who God is and who the believer is in relation to God.

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed (325 CE, refined 381 CE) is the definitive Catholic statement of Trinitarian belief. It declares the Son is “of one substance with the Father” (homoousios) — directly countering the Arian view that the Son was a created being. Catholics recite the Nicene Creed at every Mass.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question about the Trinity, you must refer to a sacred writing or source of authority — for example, Matthew 3:16–17 (baptism of Jesus), Matthew 28:19 (the Great Commission), or John 1:1 (the Word). Without naming a source, your answer cannot reach the top band.

A very common error is writing “Catholics believe in three gods.” This is the opposite of Catholic teaching. Always write “one God in three persons” or “one substance, three persons.” Knowing the word homoousios (same substance) from the Nicene Creed is a high-mark detail that rewards precise religious vocabulary.

For the 12-mark Evaluate, a strong response on the Trinity will contrast Catholic and Orthodox views (the filioque dispute) and Protestant emphasis on scripture, then weigh which understanding of the Trinity is most significant for Christian life. Always end with a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION that says which side is stronger and why — without this final paragraph you cannot reach the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic Christianity teaches that God is one in three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — not three gods. The technical phrase “one substance, three persons” (homoousios) comes from the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and is the basis of the Nicene Creed recited at every Mass.
  • The scriptural roots of the Trinity include Matthew 3:16–17 (baptism of Jesus), Matthew 28:19 (Great Commission) and John 1:1 (the Word). All three persons are distinct but inseparable — the Father creates, the Son redeems, the Holy Spirit sustains.
  • Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions all affirm the Nicene Trinity but differ on the filioque clause and on the relative authority of scripture versus Church tradition in interpreting the doctrine.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Catholic teaching about the Trinity?
A) God exists as three separate and distinct gods
B) God is one being in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit
C) The Father is the most important person and the Son and Spirit are lesser
D) The Trinity was invented by the Pope in the medieval period
practice_questions.marks: B) God is one being in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the council at which the doctrine of the Trinity was formally defined.
practice_questions.marks: The Council of Nicaea (325 CE) [1 mark]. Accept 'Nicaea' or 'the Council of Nicaea'.

practice_questions.text:
Give two ways in which belief in the Trinity influences the daily practice of Catholics.
For each way, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholics begin and end prayer with the Sign of the Cross: 'In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit' — this means that Trinitarian belief is expressed every time a Catholic prays or enters a church.
- Baptism is performed in the names of all three persons (Matthew 28:19), incorporating the new believer into a relationship with the whole Trinity.
- The Nicene Creed is recited at every Sunday Mass, meaning Catholics publicly reaffirm Trinitarian belief as a communal act of worship each week.
- The Mass is structured Trinitarianly: prayers are addressed to the Father, through the Son, in the power of the Spirit.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Nicene Creed is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons, each with precise Catholic theological knowledge; at least one clear reference to a named source (e.g. Matthew 28:19, John 1:1, the Nicene Creed itself as a named source of authority); both reasons linked to the significance for Catholic belief or practice.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, generally accurate, source reference present but not fully developed; explanation may be one-sided or lacking depth on one reason.
Developing (2 marks): One reason with some development, or two reasons briefly stated without the 'because' reasoning; limited or no source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point; no source reference; limited understanding of why the creed matters.

Acceptable points include:
- The Nicene Creed defines who God is for Catholics — it declares the Son is 'of one substance with the Father' (homoousios), countering the Arian heresy and protecting the doctrine of the Trinity; without this definition, Catholic identity would be undermined.
- The creed is a source of unity — Catholics recite it worldwide at every Mass, connecting individual believers to the global and historical Church; Matthew 28:19 grounds the Trinitarian formula the creed expresses.
- The creed encodes the scriptural Trinitarian passages (Matthew 3:16-17, John 1:1) in a precise theological formula, so believers can apply them consistently.

practice_questions.text:
'The doctrine of the Trinity is the most important belief in Catholic Christianity.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation with well-developed arguments for and against; accurate Catholic theological knowledge including named sources (Nicene Creed, Matthew 3:16-17, John 1:1); reference to contrasting Christian perspectives (Orthodox, Protestant); non-religious perspectives acknowledged where relevant; a justified conclusion stating which side is stronger and why.
Secure (7-9 marks): Most relevant points present; source reference included but not fully developed; conclusion reached but weighing of arguments not fully sustained.
Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but one-sided argument, or two sides given without development; some Catholic knowledge but generic rather than tradition-specific.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, limited source reference, listing rather than evaluating; no justified conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The Trinity is foundational — all other Catholic beliefs (incarnation, redemption, the sacraments) presuppose a Trinitarian God; without it, the identity of Jesus and the nature of salvation cannot be properly understood.
- The Nicene Creed, recited at every Mass, is entirely structured around the Trinity, suggesting the Church itself regards it as the most central belief.
- John 1:1 identifies Jesus as the eternal divine Word — if the Son were not fully God (as the creed insists), the redemption he achieves would have no ultimate power.

Arguments against:
- Catholics might argue that the Incarnation or Redemption is the most important belief because it is through Jesus's death and resurrection that salvation is made available; without the cross, the Trinity remains an abstract doctrine.
- For many Catholic believers, the practical heart of their faith is the Eucharist — described as 'the source and summit of Christian life' — rather than a metaphysical doctrine about divine persons.
- Some theologians argue that love is the core Catholic belief, since 'God is love' (1 John 4:8) and all other doctrines flow from this.

Conclusion: Candidates may reasonably conclude that the Trinity is the most important belief because it underpins all other Catholic doctrines, or that doctrines like the Incarnation are more practically central. A justified conclusion must state a reasoned preference and explain why.

practice_questions.text: Thomas is a Year 10 student preparing for Confirmation at his Catholic parish in Salford. His teacher asks him to explain what Catholics mean when they say God is a Trinity. Give two points Thomas could make.
practice_questions.marks:

lessons.title: Creation and the Dignity of the Human Person
lessons.description: Genesis 1 and 2 accounts of creation, imago Dei, stewardship and different Christian beliefs about creation.
lessons.content_html:
Two Accounts, One Message

The Bible opens with two distinct accounts of creation in Genesis 1 and Genesis 2. Catholic teaching does not require these to be read as competing stories or as a scientific textbook. Instead, the Church understands them as complementary theological accounts that reveal truths about God, the world and human beings. Genesis 1 is a majestic, structured poem in which God creates in six days and rests on the seventh. Genesis 2 is a more intimate narrative focusing on the garden, the first human, and the gift of companionship. Together they form the foundation for the Catholic understanding of creation.

Key Fact

Genesis 1 reveals that God is the source of all existence, that creation is deliberately ordered and good, and that human beings are made in God’s image (imago Dei). Genesis 2 reveals that humanity is formed from the earth yet breathed into life by God — a blend of the material and the spiritual.

Genesis 1 and the Nature of God

In Genesis 1, God creates the world through speech alone: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” This emphasises God’s absolute power and sovereignty — nothing exists independently of his will. Each stage of creation is declared “good”, and the whole is declared “very good” (Genesis 1:31). For Catholics, this teaches that the material world is not evil or fallen by nature — it is a gift from a generous Creator. The regular rhythm of six days of work and one day of rest (the Sabbath) models the pattern of human life and later becomes the basis for keeping Sunday holy in Catholic practice.

The pinnacle of Genesis 1 is the creation of humanity on the sixth day: “God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The concept of imago Dei — being made in God’s image — is central to Catholic anthropology. It means that every human being possesses inherent dignity that cannot be taken away, regardless of their social status, nationality or actions.

Genesis 2 and the Dignity of Human Beings

Genesis 2 presents a more personal creation narrative. The LORD God forms the human from the dust of the ground and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). This dual origin — from the earth and from God’s own breath — captures the Catholic understanding of human beings as both physical and spiritual creatures. The body is not a prison for the soul; both together constitute the human person.

The creation of the woman as a partner “suitable for him” (Genesis 2:18) establishes the dignity of both sexes as equally made in God’s image. Catholic teaching, drawing on Genesis 2, insists that neither man nor woman is superior — both reflect the image of God fully. The Catholic Catechism, summarising this teaching, states that human beings are the only creatures God has willed for their own sake.

Christians hold a range of views on the relationship between Genesis and modern science. Creationism (literal six-day creation) is held by some evangelical Protestant Christians, who read Genesis as historical fact. Catholic teaching since at least the papacy of Pius XII has explicitly rejected a rigid literal reading; the Church affirms that the theory of evolution is compatible with belief in God as Creator, provided one upholds that human souls are directly created by God.

Theistic evolution is the position held by most Catholic theologians and by the majority of mainstream Protestant denominations. God is the ultimate cause of the universe’s existence; the scientific account of how life developed is not in competition with the theological account of why it exists. This approach allows Catholics to accept the findings of cosmology and evolutionary biology while affirming that the universe is God’s creation and that every human being has a unique, God-given dignity.

Stewardship of Creation

Genesis 1 calls human beings to “have dominion” over the earth (Genesis 1:28). Catholic teaching interprets this not as a licence to exploit creation but as a call to stewardship — caring for the world as trustees on behalf of God. This position was reinforced by Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ (2015), a major teaching document on care for the environment, which described the earth as “our common home” and argued that the exploitation of natural resources is both an ecological and a moral problem. The document’s argument is grounded directly in the Genesis vision of creation as good and humanity as its responsible guardians.

Catholic communities across Britain today engage in environmental action inspired by this theology: parish eco-groups, fair-trade campaigns, and support for organisations such as CAFOD’s climate justice work all connect the Genesis mandate to present-day responsibility. Orthodox Christianity similarly emphasises creation care, viewing the earth as a sacrament — a means of encountering God. Protestant Christians may emphasise the dominion mandate differently, though many mainstream Protestant denominations now share the Catholic emphasis on responsible stewardship.

A common student error is to interpret “made in God’s image” as a physical resemblance — as if Genesis is claiming God has a body like ours. Catholic theology has consistently interpreted imago Dei as referring to the spiritual and moral capacities that humans share with God: reason, free will, conscience, the capacity for love and relationship. God is not a physical being; the ‘image’ is about what makes humans unique among creatures — their spiritual dimension and moral responsibility. This is a mark-scheme-distinguishing answer.

Key Fact

Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) means every human being is made in God’s image and therefore possesses inherent dignity and worth. For Catholic teaching this is the foundation of human rights, the condemnation of slavery, abortion, murder and euthanasia, and the call to treat every person as an end in themselves, never merely as a means.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on creation, you must name a sacred text. Genesis 1:27 (“God created mankind in his own image”) is the most valuable single verse you can cite: it establishes imago Dei, grounds human dignity, and supports multiple developed reasons. Always name the chapter and verse — “Genesis 1” alone is acceptable but “Genesis 1:27” demonstrates precision that rewards top-band answers.

A very common error on creation questions is treating Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 as contradictory. The exam mark scheme rewards students who explain that they are complementary theological accounts. Catholic teaching affirms that belief in God as creator is compatible with the science of evolution (theistic evolution) — knowing this contrast earns marks on a 12-mark Evaluate statement about science vs religion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 are two complementary accounts of creation. Genesis 1 reveals God’s power and declares creation ‘very good’; Genesis 2 reveals the intimate creation of the human person from earth and divine breath. Catholic teaching reads both theologically, not as a scientific alternative to evolution.
  • Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) — being made in God’s image — is the foundation of human dignity in Catholic belief. It means every human being has inherent worth, regardless of circumstance, and is the basis for Catholic social teaching on human rights.
  • Catholics understand ‘dominion’ over creation (Genesis 1:28) as stewardship — responsible care for the world as trustees on behalf of God. This teaching was developed by Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ (2015) and underpins Catholic environmental engagement today.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Catholic understanding of imago Dei?
A) Human beings physically resemble God in appearance
B) Human beings are made in God's image, giving them special dignity and moral capacity
C) Only priests and religious leaders are made in God's image
D) The concept of imago Dei means human beings are gods themselves
practice_questions.marks: B) Human beings are made in God's image, giving them special dignity and moral capacity [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one way in which Catholic teaching interprets the command to have 'dominion' over creation (Genesis 1:28).
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any of the following:
- As a call to stewardship / responsible care of creation on God's behalf.
- Not as a licence to exploit creation but as a duty to protect it.
- As trusteeship of the earth for future generations.
Do not accept 'control over animals' without reference to responsibility.

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting Christian beliefs about how to interpret the Genesis accounts of creation.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Some evangelical Protestant Christians hold a creationist or literal view: the six days in Genesis 1 are literal 24-hour days and God created the world exactly as described, making the scientific theory of evolution incompatible with Christian belief.
- Catholic teaching (and most mainstream Protestant denominations) endorses theistic evolution: God created the universe and initiated its development through natural processes; the Genesis accounts are theological, not scientific, and are compatible with evolutionary biology. The soul is directly created by God.
- Some Christians read Genesis 1 and 2 as poetry or allegory, prioritising their theological message over any historical claims.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the teaching that human beings are made in the image of God (imago Dei) is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons with precise theological knowledge; named source cited and integrated into the explanation (e.g. Genesis 1:27, Pope Francis's Laudato Si'); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic belief or practice.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate, source present but undeveloped; one reason more developed than the other.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited or no source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point; no source; generic rather than Catholic-specific.

Acceptable points include:
- Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) establishes that every human being has inherent dignity that cannot be removed — this means Catholics must oppose anything that degrades or destroys human life, from slavery to abortion, because to harm a person made in God's image is to dishonour God himself.
- It is the theological foundation of Catholic Social Teaching — the Catechism teaches that humans are the only creatures God has willed for their own sake; this grounds the Church's work for human rights, justice and the poor.
- Pope Francis's Laudato Si' (2015) connects imago Dei to environmental responsibility: because human beings uniquely bear God's image, they also uniquely bear responsibility for the rest of creation.

practice_questions.text:
'The Genesis accounts of creation are no longer relevant in a scientific age.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; Catholic position on theistic evolution explained accurately; creationist position acknowledged; non-religious/scientific view given; source references (Genesis 1:27, Laudato Si'); sub-tradition contrasts (Catholic vs evangelical Protestant); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached but not fully justified.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Modern cosmology (the Big Bang) and evolutionary biology provide comprehensive scientific accounts of the origin of the universe and life; some argue the Genesis accounts add nothing to this understanding.
- Creationist readings of Genesis have been shown to be scientifically inaccurate; if the text is not literally true, critics argue it loses its authority.
- In a secular society, basing ethics on an ancient text may seem less persuasive than grounding them in reason and human rights law.

Arguments against:
- Catholic teaching holds that Genesis answers a different question from science: not 'how' but 'why' the world exists and what human beings are for. Science cannot tell us that human beings have dignity — theology can.
- The concept of imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) continues to underpin Catholic Social Teaching, human rights advocacy, and environmental responsibility (Laudato Si', 2015) — its practical relevance is demonstrably alive.
- Theistic evolution shows the Genesis accounts and science are compatible; the Church has formally endorsed evolution while maintaining that God is the ultimate creator and source of the human soul.

Conclusion: Candidates may reasonably argue that Genesis remains highly relevant as a theological and ethical framework, or that its relevance depends on whether it is read literally or symbolically. A justified conclusion must state a reasoned preference.

practice_questions.text: Sister Maria, a Catholic Religious Education teacher at a secondary school in Birmingham, explains to her class why the Church teaches that every person has equal dignity. Give two reasons she might give, based on Catholic teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- Every human being is made in God's image (imago Dei, Genesis 1:27), giving each person inherent dignity regardless of status.
- Genesis 2 describes both man and woman as formed by God and breathed into life — neither is superior.
- Catholic teaching holds that God wills every person for their own sake, not as a means to an end.

lessons.title: Incarnation and Redemption
lessons.description: Jesus as fully God and fully human — his life, death, resurrection and ascension as the foundation of salvation.
lessons.content_html:
The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The incarnation is one of the most distinctive and central claims of Catholic Christianity: the eternal Son of God — the second person of the Trinity — entered human history as a real human being. The word comes from the Latin in carne, meaning ‘in the flesh.’ The Gospel of John expresses it directly: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us” (John 1:14). For Catholics, this is not a metaphor — Jesus of Nazareth, born of Mary in first-century Palestine, was and is fully God and fully human at the same time.

The precise phrase used by Catholic theology is that Jesus has “two natures in one person” — the divine nature and the human nature united in the single person of Christ. This was formally defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE). The two natures are “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” This means Jesus genuinely experienced human life: he was born, he grew, he felt hunger, friendship, grief and fear. Yet he also demonstrated divine knowledge, authority and power. For Catholics, both aspects are equally real and equally important.

The Incarnation is grounded in multiple scriptural sources. The opening of John’s Gospel identifies Jesus as the eternal Logos (Word) who “was with God” and “was God” (John 1:1) before becoming flesh. Matthew and Luke record the virginal conception of Jesus — Mary conceives through the Holy Spirit, not through human agency (Matthew 1:18–25, Luke 1:26–38). Paul’s letters in the New Testament reflect an early high Christology: in Philippians 2:6–8, he describes how Christ “being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.”

The Nicene Creed, recited at every Catholic Mass, captures this scriptural teaching in its definitive formula: “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven: by the power of the Holy Spirit he became incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and was made man.” The phrase “for us and for our salvation” is theologically crucial — the incarnation is not simply a divine visitation but the beginning of the redemptive work of Christ.

The Life and Ministry of Jesus

Catholics understand the entire life of Jesus, not just his death, as redemptively significant. His miracles — healing the sick, feeding the hungry, raising the dead — are signs of the coming Kingdom of God. His teachings, especially the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), articulate the values of God’s kingdom: mercy, peacemaking, justice, purity of heart. His relationships — with women, with the poor, with tax collectors and sinners — enact the inclusive love of God. For Catholics, imitating Jesus in daily life is inseparable from being saved by him.

Key Fact

The four key events through which Catholics understand redemption: (1) the life of Jesus — his teachings and miracles reveal God’s kingdom; (2) the death of Jesus on the cross — atoning sacrifice for human sin; (3) the resurrection — Jesus rises from the dead on the third day, defeating sin and death; (4) the ascension — Jesus returns to the Father, sending the Holy Spirit to be with the Church.

The Death of Jesus: Atonement and Sacrifice

The death of Jesus on the cross is understood by Catholics as an act of atonement — a sacrifice that restores the broken relationship between humanity and God caused by sin. Paul writes: “God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The sacrifice of Jesus is understood as a free act of love that meets the demands of divine justice while expressing divine mercy. Catholics believe this sacrifice is made present at every Mass through the Eucharist — one of the reasons the Mass holds such central importance in Catholic life.

Different theological traditions within Christianity have developed different models of atonement. Substitutionary atonement, emphasised in some Protestant traditions, holds that Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved in our place. Catholic theology acknowledges this dimension but tends to give equal weight to the idea of moral exemplar and to the concept of participation: through the death and resurrection of Christ, believers are drawn into a new relationship with God. The cross is not only a transaction but a revelation of God’s love.

Resurrection and Ascension

The resurrection of Jesus is the cornerstone of Catholic faith. Paul states plainly: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Catholics believe Jesus rose bodily — not as a ghost or merely spiritual presence — and was encountered by his disciples over a period of forty days. The resurrection confirms the truth of everything Jesus taught and promised, and it is the ground of Catholic hope that death is not the final word for any human being.

The ascension follows the resurrection. Jesus returns to the Father (Acts 1:9–11) and sends the Holy Spirit at Pentecost to be with the Church. For Catholics, the ascension does not mean Jesus has abandoned humanity — he remains present through the Eucharist, the Church and the Spirit. The ascension is also the basis of grace: the Holy Spirit poured out at Pentecost enables believers to share in the divine life and empowers them to live as disciples. Salvation, in Catholic understanding, is both an event (achieved on the cross) and an ongoing process (lived out through grace and the sacraments).

All three major Christian traditions teach that salvation is made possible through Jesus Christ, but they emphasise different aspects. Catholic and Orthodox Christianity understand salvation as theosis or divinisation — a gradual transformation of the believer through grace, the sacraments and a life of virtue, drawing the person into ever-deeper union with God. This is an ongoing process, not a single moment of decision.

Many Protestant traditions, particularly those in the evangelical and Reformed stream, emphasise justification by faith — that a person is declared righteous before God through faith in Christ alone, not through works or sacraments. Catholic theology accepts justification by faith but insists that genuine faith naturally produces good works, and that the sacraments are the means through which grace is communicated. The Council of Trent (1545–1563) clarified the Catholic position in response to the Protestant Reformation. In practice, all traditions agree that the death and resurrection of Jesus are the foundation of salvation.

Key Fact

Grace is God’s free gift to humanity made possible through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. In Catholic teaching, grace is communicated primarily through the seven sacraments — especially baptism (which removes original sin and begins the life of grace) and the Eucharist (which nourishes and sustains it). Grace enables the believer to do what would be impossible by human effort alone: to love as God loves, to forgive as God forgives.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question about the Incarnation or Redemption, you need a named source. Strong choices include: John 1:14 (the Word became flesh), Romans 5:8 (Christ died for us while we were sinners), 1 Corinthians 15:17 (if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile), or the Nicene Creed (“for us and for our salvation he came down from heaven”). Always name the source AND develop how it supports your reason — quoting without explanation earns fewer marks.

For the 12-mark Evaluate on redemption (e.g. “The resurrection is the most important event in the life of Jesus”), you must give arguments on both sides. Arguments for: Paul’s claim that without the resurrection faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17); it confirms Jesus’s identity and promises. Arguments against: some might argue the death/atonement is most important; or that the life and teachings of Jesus matter more in practical discipleship. End with a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION — state which side you find more persuasive and explain why.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Incarnation means the eternal Son of God became human in Jesus of Nazareth — fully God and fully human, defined at Chalcedon (451 CE). John 1:14 and the Nicene Creed are the key sources. The purpose, as the creed states, is “for us and for our salvation.”
  • Redemption unfolds through the four key events: Jesus’s life (reveals God’s kingdom), his death (atonement for sin — Romans 5:8), his resurrection (defeats death — 1 Corinthians 15:17), and his ascension (sends the Holy Spirit and grace). Catholics believe all four are redemptively significant.
  • Grace is God’s free gift to humanity, made possible through Christ and communicated through the sacraments. Salvation in Catholic teaching is both an event (the cross) and an ongoing process (life in grace). This differs from many Protestant traditions, which emphasise a single moment of justification by faith.

practice_questions.marks: B) The eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus of Nazareth while remaining fully God [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the event in which Jesus returned to the Father forty days after the resurrection.
practice_questions.marks: The Ascension [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Christian beliefs about how the death of Jesus brings salvation.
For each belief, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholic teaching understands the death of Jesus as an act of atonement — a sacrifice that restores the broken relationship between humanity and God; this sacrifice is made present at every Mass through the Eucharist, which is why the Mass is central to Catholic life.
- Many Protestant traditions emphasise substitutionary atonement — Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved in humanity's place; this means salvation is received through faith in what Christ did, not through sacraments or works.
- Orthodox Christianity sees the cross as the victory of life over death and the beginning of theosis — transformation into the divine life; salvation is a process of becoming more Christlike rather than a legal transaction.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the resurrection of Jesus is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; at least one named source integrated into the argument (e.g. 1 Corinthians 15:17, John 1:14, the Nicene Creed); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic belief or life.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source present but partially developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- The resurrection confirms the truth of everything Jesus taught and promised — Paul states 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17); without the resurrection, the Christian hope of salvation would have no foundation.
- The resurrection is the basis of Catholic hope for life after death — because Jesus rose bodily, Catholics believe that they too will share in resurrection; this transforms how Catholics approach death and gives meaning to suffering.
- The resurrection confirms the identity of Jesus as the Son of God and validates his atoning death — the Nicene Creed celebrates 'on the third day he rose again', making the resurrection central to Trinitarian faith.

practice_questions.text:
'The death of Jesus on the cross is more important than his resurrection for Catholic Christians.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; accurate Catholic teaching on atonement, resurrection, ascension; named sources (Romans 5:8, 1 Corinthians 15:17, John 1:14, Nicene Creed); sub-tradition contrast (Catholic vs Protestant on atonement models); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Paul's language in Romans 5:8 focuses on the sacrificial death as the moment of reconciliation: 'Christ died for us.' The Mass re-presents this sacrifice — suggesting the death is the pivotal act.
- Some theological traditions (e.g. substitutionary atonement, prominent in evangelical Protestantism) emphasise that the cross is where sin is dealt with; the resurrection confirms this but does not achieve it.
- Catholic devotional life (the Stations of the Cross, the crucifix in every church) focuses heavily on the passion and death, suggesting the death holds particular weight.

Arguments against:
- Paul also insists: 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17) — without the resurrection, the death has no ultimate power.
- The resurrection is the basis of hope for believers — it shows that death is not the end and that Jesus's redemptive work is complete and victorious.
- Catholic teaching on grace and salvation is grounded in the risen Christ sending the Spirit; without the resurrection and ascension, there would be no Church, no sacraments, and no ongoing communication of grace.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion will acknowledge that Catholics themselves hold both together: 'We proclaim your death, O Lord, and profess your resurrection' (the Memorial Acclamation at Mass), suggesting neither alone is sufficient.

practice_questions.text: Caitlin is a Catholic teenager attending Mass with her family at a parish in Liverpool. She notices the large crucifix at the front of the church. Give two reasons why the crucifix is an important symbol in a Catholic church.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- It represents the atoning death of Jesus — the sacrifice that reconciles humanity to God.
- It is a reminder of God's love for humanity — 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8).
- It keeps the passion of Jesus at the centre of Catholic worship and devotion.
- It reminds Catholics that the Mass re-presents the sacrifice of the cross.

lessons.title: Life After Death and the Seven Sacraments
lessons.description: Resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and purgatory, and the names, meanings and effects of the seven sacraments.
lessons.content_html:
What Happens After Death?

Catholic Christianity teaches that death is not the end of the human person. Because Jesus rose from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), Catholics believe that all human beings will one day share in a resurrection of the body. The Nicene Creed declares: “We look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.” This is not a vague idea of the soul floating away — Catholic teaching insists that the whole person, body and soul, will be raised.

After death, Catholic teaching describes a process involving personal judgement, then either heaven, hell or purgatory, followed at the end of time by a final or “Last” Judgement. The Catechism summarises: each person receives a retribution of their souls in the particular judgement immediately after death. The Last Judgement at the end of time will confirm this verdict before all people and before the whole of creation.

Key Fact

Four key elements of Catholic belief about life after death: (1) Resurrection — the whole person (body and soul) will be raised; (2) Judgement — a personal judgement immediately after death and a Last Judgement at the end of time; (3) Heaven — eternal life with God; (4) Purgatory — a process of purification before heaven; Hell is the consequence of a definitive rejection of God’s love.

Heaven, Hell and Purgatory

Heaven is the Catholic term for the perfect communion with God. It is not primarily a physical place but a state of being — the beatific vision, the experience of knowing God directly and fully. Jesus promises: “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (John 14:2). Heaven is the fulfilment of the deepest human longing and the goal of all grace and sacramental life.

Hell is the state of permanent separation from God. Catholic teaching insists that hell is real and that it is the result of a person’s own free choice to reject God definitively. Jesus himself speaks of hell in the Gospels (e.g. Matthew 25:41). The Church does not name any individual as being in hell, and Pope John Paul II emphasised that hell is not so much a punishment imposed by God as a consequence that persons bring on themselves by their choices.

Purgatory is a distinctively Catholic teaching (not held by most Protestant Christians). It refers to a process of purification for those who die in a state of grace but have not yet fully shed their attachment to sin. The Catholic Catechism teaches that those in purgatory are certainly saved — purgatory is not a second chance at salvation — but they undergo a process that prepares them for the full joy of heaven. Catholics pray for those in purgatory, particularly on the feast of All Souls (2 November).

Most Protestant denominations reject the doctrine of purgatory, arguing that it has no clear basis in the Bible and that Christ’s atoning death is fully sufficient — no further purification is needed after death. Protestants generally teach that at death, the saved enter immediately into the presence of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:8: “to be away from the body and at home with the Lord”). Prayers for the dead are not a feature of most Protestant practice.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity shares much Catholic teaching about life after death — resurrection, judgement, heaven and a form of continued development toward God after death — but uses different terminology, speaking of “the toll houses” rather than purgatory, and understands the process through the lens of deification (theosis) rather than legal purification. Orthodox Christians also pray for the dead.

What Is a Sacrament?

The word sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, meaning a solemn pledge or sacred action. For Catholics, a sacrament is an outward, physical sign that was instituted by Christ and through which God communicates grace. The physical actions — water poured, oil anointed, bread and wine consecrated — are not mere symbols. They actually convey what they signify. Catholic theology speaks of the “sacramental nature of reality”: the material world is capable of mediating the divine.

There are seven sacraments in Catholic teaching, divided into three groups: sacraments of initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), sacraments of healing (Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick), and sacraments of service (Holy Orders, Matrimony). The Eucharist holds the supreme place: Catholic teaching describes it as “the source and summit of Christian life” — all other sacraments and all Christian activity flows from and leads back to the Mass.

Key Fact

The seven sacraments: Baptism (removes original sin, initiates into the Church), Confirmation (strengthens faith, gifts of the Holy Spirit), Eucharist (source and summit of Christian life; real presence of Christ), Reconciliation (forgiveness of sin), Anointing of the Sick (healing and comfort in illness), Holy Orders (ordination of deacons, priests and bishops), Matrimony (marriage as a lifelong covenant).

The Eucharist: Source and Summit

The Eucharist (the Mass) holds a unique place among the seven sacraments. Catholic teaching holds the doctrine of transubstantiation: at the consecration, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, even though the outward appearances (taste, texture) remain. This was formally defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at the Council of Trent (1551). The scriptural basis is the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26–28; Luke 22:19–20) and John 6:51: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Most Protestant Christians do not hold the doctrine of transubstantiation. Many regard the Eucharist as a memorial or symbolic act of remembrance (as Zwingli, a sixteenth-century Swiss reformer, taught) rather than an actual change in the elements. Some Protestant traditions (notably Lutheran) hold a doctrine of “real presence” that does not go as far as transubstantiation. Eastern Orthodox Christianity teaches that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist but has not adopted the specific philosophical language of transubstantiation. For Catholics, this difference about the Eucharist is one of the most significant points of divergence among Christian traditions.

Baptism is the first and foundational sacrament. Catholic teaching holds that all human beings are born with original sin — the consequence of the first human disobedience described in Genesis 3 — which creates a barrier between humanity and God. Baptism, in which water is poured three times in the name of the Trinity, removes original sin and initiates the person into the Church. It is the door to all the other sacraments.

Most Protestant traditions also practise baptism but differ on its effects. Some (e.g. Baptist, evangelical) insist baptism must be chosen by a believing adult (believer’s baptism) and regard it as an outward sign of inward faith rather than a sacrament that confers grace. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican traditions generally baptise infants, believing that baptism itself communicates grace and removes original sin regardless of the recipient’s age or choice.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on the sacraments, do not simply list all seven. The exam asks you to “explain two reasons why the sacraments are important” or “explain two contrasting Christian views about the Eucharist.” Pick one or two sacraments and develop them fully. The strongest answers reference the Eucharist and the phrase “source and summit of Christian life” — plus a scriptural source such as Matthew 26:26–28 (Last Supper) or John 6:51 (I am the living bread). Name the source and develop your reason using ‘because’ or ‘this means that.’

On the 12-mark Evaluate question about life after death (e.g. “Belief in purgatory is the most important Catholic belief about life after death”), remember that Protestant Christians reject purgatory while Catholics defend it. Arguments FOR will use Catholic Catechism teaching and prayer for the dead; arguments AGAINST will use Protestant “justification by faith” and the Bible alone argument. Always end with a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholic belief about life after death includes bodily resurrection, personal judgement, and the three possible destinations: heaven (eternal life with God), purgatory (purification for those who die in grace but not fully ready), and hell (eternal separation from God by one’s own free choice). Purgatory is distinctive to Catholicism; most Protestant traditions reject it.
  • The seven sacraments are physical signs instituted by Christ through which God communicates grace. They are grouped as initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), healing (Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick) and service (Holy Orders, Matrimony). The Eucharist is described as “the source and summit of Christian life.”
  • The doctrine of transubstantiation — that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ at the consecration — distinguishes the Catholic understanding of the Eucharist from most Protestant views, which see the Eucharist as memorial or symbolic rather than a real change in the elements.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation?
A) The bread and wine are symbols of Jesus's body and blood
B) Jesus is spiritually but not physically present in the Eucharist
C) The substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ at the consecration
D) The Eucharist is a re-enactment of the Last Supper but nothing actually changes
practice_questions.marks: C) The substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ at the consecration [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Catholic sacrament described as 'the source and summit of Christian life'.
practice_questions.marks: The Eucharist (also accept 'the Mass') [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Give two contrasting Christian beliefs about what happens after death.
For each belief, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholic teaching includes belief in purgatory — a process of purification for those who die in God's grace but are not yet ready for heaven; Catholics therefore pray for the souls of the dead, particularly on All Souls' Day.
- Most Protestant Christians reject purgatory, arguing that Christ's atoning death is fully sufficient — at death, those who have faith enter immediately into the presence of God (2 Corinthians 5:8); praying for the dead is therefore not a Protestant practice.
- Orthodox Christianity teaches ongoing development toward God after death (theosis) but uses different terminology from purgatory.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the seven sacraments are important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; at least one named source (e.g. Matthew 26:26-28 for the Eucharist, John 6:51, the Nicene Creed); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic life.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- The sacraments are the primary means through which God communicates grace to believers — without the sacraments, Catholics believe they would be cut off from the divine life; baptism removes original sin and initiates believers into the Church, making all subsequent sacramental life possible.
- The Eucharist, described as 'the source and summit of Christian life', makes the sacrifice of Christ present at every Mass (Matthew 26:26-28: 'This is my body... this is my blood'); this means Catholics can participate directly in Christ's redemptive act week by week.
- Reconciliation (confession) restores the relationship with God broken by serious sin — it reflects Jesus's words to the disciples: 'If you forgive anyone's sins, their sins are forgiven' (John 20:23).

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in purgatory is the most important Catholic teaching about life after death.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; accurate Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and purgatory; Protestant rejection of purgatory cited and developed; named sources (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, the Nicene Creed, Catechism teaching); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source included; conclusion reached but weighing of arguments incomplete.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Purgatory is distinctively Catholic — it shapes a range of practices (prayer for the dead, indulgences, masses for the souls of the deceased) that are absent from Protestant Christianity; it could be argued that this makes it uniquely defining for Catholic identity.
- Purgatory expresses the Catholic belief in God's mercy toward those who have tried to live well but are imperfect — it offers hope for the majority of believers who are not fully ready for heaven at death.
- The doctrine shapes how Catholics grieve: the practice of praying for the dead (especially on All Souls' Day) gives a practical dimension to belief that is absent if purgatory is rejected.

Arguments against:
- The resurrection is arguably more foundational — the Nicene Creed, which Catholics recite at every Mass, includes 'we look for the resurrection of the dead' but does not mention purgatory; resurrection is thus doctrinally more central.
- Most Protestant Christians reject purgatory entirely, regarding it as lacking biblical support; this means it is a divisive rather than a unifying belief and might not be 'most important' if measured by breadth of Christian agreement.
- For many Catholics, the belief in heaven — eternal communion with God — is more important because it is the ultimate destination and the source of Christian hope.

Conclusion: Candidates may reasonably argue either side. A strong conclusion acknowledges that purgatory is distinctive to Catholicism but that the resurrection and heaven are more central to the Catholic creed as recited at Mass.

practice_questions.text: Patrick is preparing to receive the sacrament of Confirmation at his Catholic parish in Manchester. Give two effects that Confirmation is believed to have, according to Catholic teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- Confirmation strengthens the faith received at baptism.
- It is believed to confer the gifts of the Holy Spirit on the recipient.
- It completes the initiation into the Church begun at baptism.
- It equips the confirmed Catholic to be a witness to their faith in the world.

glossary_terms.definition: In Catholic teaching, an outward sign instituted by Christ that confers grace — a physical action through which God communicates divine life to believers.
The central Catholic sacrament in which, through the consecration of bread and wine, Catholics believe the body and blood of Jesus Christ become truly present.
The Catholic doctrine that at the consecration of the Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Jesus Christ, while the appearances of bread and wine remain.
In Catholic belief, a process of purification after death for those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully ready for heaven.
In Catholic belief, the state of eternal life with God, characterised by the beatific vision — seeing God face to face.
In Catholic belief, the state of eternal separation from God, resulting from a definitive rejection of God's love during earthly life.
In Catholic belief, the bodily rising of the dead at the end of time, modelled on the resurrection of Jesus.
The state of inherited sinfulness understood in Catholic teaching as the consequence of the first human disobedience, affecting all people from birth.
